newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: YEAR - Pakistan sugar imports seen up as production lags.
newsitem.headline: YEAR - Pakistan sugar imports seen up as production lags.

text.p: Pakistan's sugar imports are likely to soar next year amid waning domestic production and rising consumption, analysts say.
Sugar demand is growing in Pakistan, where the population is expanding about three percent a year, and in neighbouring Iran and Afghanistan, from where it is smuggled to Central Asia.
"Total sugar imports in 1996/97 (July-June), including 375,000 tonnes ordered by October, are likely to be around 750,000 tonnes," said one mill owner.
Pakistan imported only 3,452 tonnes of sugar in 1995/96. Imports reached 254,603 tonnes in July-October 1996, compared to 406 tonnes in the year-ago period, official figures show.

Anticipating a shortfall due to a late start to the current sugarcane crushing season, Pakistan is seeking 50,000 tonnes of crystal white sugar ahead of the Moslem fasting month of Ramadan starting next month, when consumption usually surges.
The state-run Trading Corporation of Pakistan (TCP) opened the bids earlier this month but has yet to make a decision.

The mill owner, who asked not to be identified, said mills had produced only 140,000 tonnes of sugar by November 30, compared to 390,000 tonnes a year ago. The figures could not immediately be confirmed from the Pakistan Sugar Mills Association.

Altaf Saleem, a former chairman of the association, said the crushing season was now in full swing and it was a poor time to import sugar. "The situation is not so bad as to compel the government to import sugar," he said.
Apart from the 50,000 tonnes Pakistan is seeking for shipment by December 31, the TCP has already imported 225,000 tonnes and private traders have brought in a further 150,000.
The millowner said sugar production had dropped due to higher excise duty, a smaller sugarcane crop, high sugarcane prices and sales tax on previously-exempt bagasse, or pulp left after crushing.
Another major factor, he said, was a switch by many farmers into production of tax-free gur, an unrefined brown sugar product much in demand in Central Asia and Afghanistan.

Gur is now selling for about 22 rupees ($0.55) per kg and requires fewnnes in 1995/96, 800,000 tonnes in 1993/94 and 600,000 tonnes in 1992/93, an executive of the Pakistan Sugar Mills Association said.
Ali Qizilbash, its secretary general, said he expected Pakistan to produce 2.65 million tonnes of sugar in 1996/97 from 30.2 million tonnes of sugarcane, crushed at 74 mills.
This would be enough to meet consumption estimated at 2.6 million tonnes, he added.
Salem, chief executive of Shakarganj Sugar Mills, felt the sugar output dived nearly 22 percent to 2.46 million tonnes in 1995/96 from 2.99 million tonnes in 1994/95.
A mill owner attributed the fall partly to a drop in the sugar recovery rate to 9.19 percent from 9.65 in 1994/95.
He said sugar prices were likely to jump to 26 rupees per kg from 22 now in the open market and 16 at state-run U also risen due to an increase in fuel prices.
The government has fixed mill-gate sugar prices at 20.75 rupees per kg in Sindh province and 21.50 in Punjab province.
